opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the opportunity is actually enormous, and it's one of the things I'm most excited about right now.

Generative AI models are fundamentally statistical. They're extraordinarily good at producing things that *look* right: fluent text, plausible code, reasonable-sounding answers. But "looks right" and "is right" are different things, and for a lot of applications that gap really matters. If you're asking a model about your company's HR policy, whether an access control configuration is secure, or whether a piece of code does what it's supposed to do, you don't want something that's probably correct. You want an answer you can trust, and ideally one you can check.

Automated reasoning, which is the field I've spent my career in, is about using mathematical logic to prove things about systems. Over the last couple of decades the tools have gotten dramatically better. SAT solvers, SMT solvers, theorem provers, model checkers can now handle problems at a scale that would have seemed impossible twenty years ago. In industry we've been using them to prove properties of cryptography, of policy languages, of storage systems, of networking configurations, and so on.

So the opportunity, as I see it, comes in a few flavors.

The first is using automated reasoning as a check on the output of generative models. The language model does the creative, fuzzy work of translating between natural language and something more formal, and then the reasoning engine verifies whether the result is actually consistent with the rules, the policy, or the specification. If it isn't, you can tell the user, or feed the counterexample back to the model and have it try again. That gives you a kind of guardrail that isn't just another statistical model guessing whether the first one was wrong. It's grounded in logic.

The second is the other direction: generative AI helping automated reasoning. Historically, one of the big bottlenecks in formal methods has been that writing specifications and proofs is hard. It takes specialists, and there just aren't that many of us. Language models turn out to be quite good at proposing proof steps, invariants, lemmas, and draft specifications. The nice thing is that the proof checker doesn't care where the proof came from. If the model hallucinates a bad proof step, the checker rejects it. So you get the creativity of the model with the soundness of the prover. That's a really powerful combination, and I think it could democratize formal verification in a way we've wanted for a long time.

The third, and maybe the most interesting, is the agentic setting. As we move toward AI systems that take actions on our behalf, calling APIs, changing configurations, moving money, the question of "can I trust this?" becomes much more acute. Automated reasoning gives you a way to state, precisely, what an agent is and isn't allowed to do, and then actually prove that its behavior stays within those bounds, rather than hoping it does.

There are real challenges, of course. The hardest part is often not the reasoning itself but the translation: getting from ambiguous human language to a precise formal statement that actually captures what people meant. People often don't agree on what a policy means until you force them to be precise. But that's also where the two fields complement each other so nicely. So I think we're at a moment where neurosymbolic approaches, combining the learned and the logical, go from an academic idea to something that really matters in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the opportunity is actually quite large, and it comes from the fact that these two fields are, in a sense, perfect complements of each other.

Generative AI, large language models in particular, are incredibly good at the things automated reasoning has always been bad at. They're creative, they're flexible, they can take a vague, natural-language description of a problem and produce something plausible. But "plausible" is the key word. They have no inherent notion of truth. They're probabilistic machines, and the thing that makes them so capable is also the thing that makes them hallucinate.

Automated reasoning is the opposite. It's the branch of AI that's about logic and proof. You take a mathematical model of a system, you take a property you care about, and you use a tool to either find a proof that the property holds or find a counterexample showing it doesn't. The results are sound. When a theorem prover or an SMT solver says something is true, it's true, and you can check the proof independently. The weakness is that those tools are brittle. You need an expert to formalize the problem, and the tools don't help you much with the creative part of figuring out what to prove or how to structure the argument.

So the first opportunity is using automated reasoning as a check on generative AI. If a model produces code, we can ask a verifier whether that code actually satisfies a specification. If a model makes a claim about, say, what an access control policy allows, we can translate the question into logic and get a definitive answer rather than a guess. At AWS we've been doing this kind of thing for years in services like IAM Access Analyzer and in the networking stack, and what's changed is that now we have a powerful front end that can take messy human intent and get it into a form the reasoning engines can work with. You get the fluency of the language model with the soundness of the solver underneath, and the model is prevented from confidently asserting things that are false.

The second opportunity runs the other direction. For decades, the hardest part of formal verification has been the human effort: writing specifications, finding loop invariants, constructing proofs, picking the right abstractions. Those are exactly the kind of search-and-pattern-matching tasks that language models are turning out to be good at. A model can propose a hundred candidate invariants, and it doesn't matter if ninety-nine are wrong, because the prover will reject them in milliseconds and accept the one that works. The combination is a loop where the generative side proposes and the reasoning side disposes. That could dramatically lower the cost of applying formal methods, which has always been the thing holding the field back.

And then there's a third, more speculative piece, which is that I think this gives us a path toward AI systems we can actually trust in high-stakes settings. If you're going to let a model take actions in production, you want guardrails that are more than just another model saying "that looks fine." You want a formal policy, and a checker that can prove the proposed action complies with it. Logic gives you that kind of guarantee. Statistics alone never will.

So the short version is: generative AI gives us a way to bridge the gap between humans and formal tools, and formal tools give us a way to bridge the gap between generative AI and truth. Putting those together is, I think, one of the most interesting things happening in computing right now.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a tremendous opportunity to combine the strengths of the two. Generative AI is very good at proposing things—a piece of code, an explanation, a possible solution. Automated reasoning gives us a way to check whether those proposals actually satisfy some precise requirement.

Take code generation. A model can produce a program that looks plausible, but does it do what you intended? Does it handle all the relevant inputs? If we can express those requirements formally, we can use automated reasoning to check the program. And when the check fails, we can give the model a counterexample and ask it to try again. So you get this loop of generation, checking, and refinement.

The important qualification is that the guarantee is about the property you specified, under the assumptions you made. It doesn’t magically make everything the model says true. But for problems where we can state what correctness means, it’s a really exciting way to turn a powerful generator into something we can use with much greater confidence.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a really exciting opportunity to combine the creativity of generative AI with the rigor of automated reasoning. A language model can propose a solution, and then a reasoning tool can check whether that solution satisfies a precise set of requirements.

Take code generation. Producing code that looks plausible is one thing; establishing that it has the properties you need is another. If you can express those properties formally, you can use automated reasoning to check the generated code. When the check fails, the tool may give you a counterexample that you can feed back to the model so it can try again.

The challenge is that you have to get the specification right, too. Proving that a program meets the wrong specification doesn’t solve your problem. But that’s another place where generative AI could help: helping people articulate what they want in a form that these tools can reason about. So I see a productive loop between generating candidates, checking them, and refining them.
